# Louse- and flea-borne diseases

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Zoonoses and vector-borne diseases > Louse- and flea-borne diseases*

[Original Article Link](/library/mH0VIh)

---

## Summary

<u>Louse</u>- and <u>flea-borne diseases</u> are caused by pathogens that are transmitted by <u>lice</u> or <u>fleas</u>. The most dangerous <u>flea-borne diseases</u> are <u>plague</u> and <u>murine typhus</u>.

---

## Louse-borne diseases

<u>Epidemic typhus</u> is a <u>louse-borne disease</u> that is described separately in “<u>Typhus</u>.”




### Trench fever (<u>five-day fever</u>)




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: most commonly affects people who are at risk of body <u>louse</u> <u>infestation</u> (e.g., homeless)

* Etiology: <u>Bartonella quintana</u>

* Transmission: : feces of infected body <u>louse</u> (<u>vector</u>)

* Clinical features

* <u>Recurrent fever</u> episodes that last ∼ 5 days

* Nonspecific, <u>flu-like</u> symptoms (<u>malaise</u>, <u>headache</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>)

* Bone <u>pain</u>, <u>splenomegaly</u>, and <u>maculopapular rash</u> of the trunk may occur

* Diagnostics: isolation of <u>Bartonella</u> confirms the diagnosis

* <u>Bartonella</u> is difficult to grow on culture

* <u>Serology</u> testing or <u>PCR</u> are often necessary

* Treatment: <u>doxycycline</u> PLUS <u>gentamicin</u>





### Louse-borne relapsing fever




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: most common in areas affected by overcrowding, war, refugee camps

* <u>Pathogen</u>: <u>Borrelia recurrentis</u>

* Transmission: : feces of infected body <u>louse</u> (<u>vector</u>)

* Clinical features

* Recurring episodes of high <u>fever</u> (102.2–109.4 °F) lasting 3–6 days followed by an afebrile period of 7 days

* Other symptoms include <u>headache</u>, <u>arthralgia</u>, <u>nausea</u>, confusion, <u>macular rash</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: detection of <u>B. recurrentis</u> in <u>peripheral blood smear</u>, <u>bone marrow</u>, or <u>CSF</u> with Wright or <u>Giemsa stain</u>

* Culture is difficult

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: <u>normocytic anemia</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u> , ↑ <u>ESR</u>

* Treatment

* <u>Doxycycline</u> OR <u>ceftriaxone</u>

* Children and pregnant woman: <u>amoxicillin</u> and <u>cefuroxime</u>





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Borrelia</u> recurentis causes a recurrent (relapsing) <u>fever</u>.

---

## Flea-borne diseases

<u>Murine typhus</u> is described separately in “<u>Typhus</u>.” <u>Dipylidiasis</u> is described separately in "<u>Helminth infections</u>."




### Plague




#### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[1]](/library/KxWUxn0)




* <u>Endemic</u> in the Western US as sporadic cases in rural areas

* Certain foci in Asia (e.g., India), South America, and sub-Saharan Africa (e.g., Madagascar)





#### Etiology [[1]](/library/KxWUxn0)[[2]](/library/19W2mn0)




* <u>Pathogen</u>: <u>Yersinia pestis</u>

* Reservoir: : prairie dogs, squirrels, rodents

* Transmission

* Bites by infected <u>fleas</u> (most common)

* Rarely: contact with tissue or respiratory droplets from an infected animal or human  [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Y. pestis</u> is considered a <u>pathogen</u> of the highest concern because of its potential use as a bioweapon. [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)




#### Clinical features [[1]](/library/KxWUxn0)[[2]](/library/19W2mn0)




The signs and symptoms of <u>plague</u> depend on the clinical form of the disease.




* <u>Incubation period</u>: 1–8 days [[1]](/library/KxWUxn0)[[2]](/library/19W2mn0)

* Bubonic plague (most common)

* Symptoms of bubonic plague include sudden onset of <u>fever</u>, <u>headache</u>, <u>myalgias</u>, chills, and painful <u>swollen lymph nodes</u> (<u>buboes</u>)

* May progress to <u>sepsis</u>, <u>pneumonia</u>, and <u>meningitis</u>

* Pneumonic plague 

* Symptoms of pneumonic plague overlap with <u>symptoms of pneumonia</u> (e.g., <u>fever</u>, <u>dyspnea</u>, productive <u>cough</u>) [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)

* Rapid progression with possible <u>respiratory failure</u> and <u>shock</u> if untreated

* Septicemic plague: <u>clinical features of sepsis</u>, possible <u>shock</u>, gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>), acral <u>gangrene</u>, without <u>localizing signs</u>   [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)[[1]](/library/KxWUxn0)

* Rare forms: meningeal , pharyngeal  [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)





![Acral gangrene in septicemic plague](media/n2nwuqahtkt3qgiwbj6djq6b.jpg)

Acral gangrene in septicemic plague




#### Diagnosis of plague [[1]](/library/KxWUxn0)[[3]](/library/w2ahPP)




Suspect <u>plague</u> in patients with concerning clinical features who report recent travel to <u>endemic</u> areas or contact with rodents or other <u>vectors</u>. Diagnosis is confirmed if <u>Y. pestis</u> is detected on microscopy or culture or the F1 <u>antigen</u> of <u>Y. pestis</u> is detected on <u>serology</u>.




* Microbiology

* Bacterial cultures from blood, <u>sputum</u>, <u>CSF</u>, or <u>bubo</u> <u>aspirate</u> depending on the presentation

* Direct visualization and staining on microscopy

* Wayson stain: bipolar staining of bacteria (“closed safety pin” appearance)

* <u>Gram stain</u>: small <u>gram-negative coccobacilli</u>

* <u>Serology</u>: detects <u>antibodies</u> to F1 <u>antigen</u> of <u>Y. pestis</u>  [[3]](/library/w2ahPP)

* Rapid tests: detect F1 <u>antigen</u>; highly sensitive and can be used to support diagnosis in remote areas [[4]](/library/oxW0xn0)[[5]](/library/6xWjxn0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Plague</u> is a nationally <u>notifiable disease</u>. [[1]](/library/KxWUxn0)




![Yersinia pestis](media/fimix5hn5vbihkeidd20fred.jpg)

Yersinia pestis




#### Treatment of plague [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)




Immediately start <u>antibiotic therapy</u> for 10–14 days. [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)




* Bubonic or pharyngeal <u>plague</u>

* First-line: <u>fluoroquinolones</u>, e.g., <u>ciprofloxacin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE, <u>doxycycline</u> DOSAGE, or <u>aminoglycosides</u>, e.g., <u>gentamicin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)

* Second-line: <u>chloramphenicol</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)

* Pneumonic or <u>septicemic plague</u>

* First-line: <u>fluoroquinolones</u>, e.g., <u>ciprofloxacin</u> DOSAGE, or <u>aminoglycosides</u>, e.g., <u>gentamicin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)

* Second-line: <u>tetracyclines</u>, e.g., <u>doxycycline</u> DOSAGE [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)

* <u>Plague</u> <u>meningitis</u>: <u>chloramphenicol</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE or <u>fluoroquinolones</u>, e.g., <u>levofloxacin</u> DOSAGE [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)





> [!WARNING]
> Do not delay treatment for diagnostics. [[3]](/library/w2ahPP)




#### Prevention of plague [[1]](/library/KxWUxn0)[[2]](/library/19W2mn0)




* <u>Infection control</u>: Implement <u>droplet precautions</u> for patients with <u>pneumonic plague</u>.

* <u>Postexposure prophylaxis</u>: Consider for individuals who have had direct contact with a person with <u>pneumonic plague</u>, an infected animal, or infectious materials.

* <u>Doxycycline</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)

* OR a <u>fluoroquinolone</u>, e.g., <u>ciprofloxacin</u> DOSAGE [[2]](/library/19W2mn0)

* <u>Vaccination</u> is not currently available in the US.
